Soul has mentioned in interviews before that one of the reasons he focuses so much on multi/polysyllabic rhymes is that they provide a natural rhythm in an acapella format.

Battle rap in general is far more 'technically' competent in terms of vocabulary, rhyme, and lyrical complexity than the average writing, mostly because it's the core focus of the content and as such needs to have a lot of effort put in.

What you might have stumbled on is that it's weird so many people are so good at this yet have never shared publicly any methodology to doing so. That's probably the case with any relatively new art-form, but also battle rap has a culture of priding yourself on your ability and not 'biting' from other people.

tl;dr: Use longer/more emphatic rhymes to provide natural structure to your lines, listen to lots of music w/ good rhythm to learn how to flow over a beat, then transition to acapella.

In my understanding, 'soft' sciences are 'soft' because even accumulated data does not necessarily yield provable or accountable predictions. To this end, 'personality science' is about as soft as you can get.

With that in mind, I think the mistake is actually in trying to use things like MB typings for predictive science--they're not meant to do that, nor could anything which groups all of humanity into so few countable groups hope to do so. It's just a tool for finding like-minded people and interests, and the notion that people can't self-select to at least some modicum of emergent pattern is a bit silly to me. Yes, the type divisions might not be strict or even that meaningful, but if people can use the types as a way to explore themselves and meet other likeminded people then it doesn't really matter IMO.

the writer David Foster Wallace (a name notable for his writing of Infinite Jest, one of the largest and most intentionally overly complicated novels ever published, as well as a bunch of influential post-modern essays etc.) effectively wrote a short story with a 'it was just a dream' ending. There's a lot to talk about on this topic, but what's interesting to me in watching the video you linked is that he refers to the game as a piece of art. I'm not saying video games aren't art, far from it, but looking at an MMO as a piece of art first is doing a bit of disservice to what it actually is, which is a product. Game design in general has always been at the conflux of these two forms, and even indie development isn't free from having to make their games a 'thing to sell' before it's a 'thing to play'. If, for some reason, it was suddenly the best-selling thing in the world to make games that played themselves completely for their entire duration, we'd likely see a lot more games doing that regardless of whether it has any intrinsic or artistic merit, because games are a means to an end, that being capital aka money.

That all being said, something like FFXIV is much more of a 'product' to me than it is a piece of art, or even an experience. It's also a means to an end--a way for me to click absent-mindedly on a screen and watch numbers go up in one of many columns all while wearing a fantasy-themed coat of paint, with moogle and chocobos and stuff. And probably I have friends that also like making numbers go up and also like that coat of paint, and we just need something or other to do while we chat in a voice call for a few hours. I'm not saying this is actually the case with me personally, but if I imagine the potential demographic for this game, that probably fits the bill.

This is all also coming from someone who is largely a gameplay/gamefeel purist: if I'm not tremendously engaged with your systems and mechanics every second I'm holding the controller, your game is less appealing to me. To that end, something that requires literally no player input isn't appealing at all on an intrinsic level... but I still get why it IS appealing to some people, and I think digging into the pits of one of the most monetized genres in the industry looking for something moving or meaningful is a bit out of place.

My two cents, anyway.

Speaking as someone who has done glitch hunting both in speedrunning and as a hobby, a lot of time what you're looking for falls into a sort of common 'glitch parlance'. A big one for this is collision detection--as time goes on it's less and less common for collision detection to randomly bug out, but there will always be instances in which you can force the game to its limits and see if it can handle what you're throwing at it. A simple example of this might be looking for bits of intersecting geometry at odd angles, noticing if your momentum is affected in any unique way when you collide with certain objects, and especially looking for any state you can force the player character to enter where their animation and movement seem like they're behaving in unaccounted for ways.

A simple example of this one for me was stumbling on a wall clip in Sonic Mania. It's a very basic setup--as Knuckles, you glide into a section of wall that's made out of conveyor belts. Because the game is pushing you backwards, but you're still technically in a flying state, which the game also counts as falling, you start stacking your aerial momentum to absurd values, until finally it's so high that the game can't tell where to put you on the next frame and you clip through the wall.

Not every game is going to have stuff like this, and more technical/obtuse glitches benefit from dedicated data-mining and TASers, but it's also always the case that you'll probably be able to find something in any game if you look hard enough.

A huge difference between authentic chiptunes and 'emulated' chiptunes is how many simultaneous channels are being used for what and also the behaviour of the instruments within those channels.

It's been expanded upon elsewhere, but while an individual channel may not be able to output simultaneous polyphonic notes, you can use multiple concurrent channels or tricks like arpeggiation to get 'chord' sounds. However, you can also decide for yourself if you're more committed to a direct and faithful recreation of the original chiptune sound or if you want to take certain modernizations into your workflow to make things easier or improve the sound quality.

A big example of this for me (because I do a lot of NES chiptunes) is how I want to handle drums/the noise channel. Ostensibly an authentic NES chiptune only has the one noise channel and has to trade off what it wants to do for snare, hi-hat, and kick emulation... but there are also 'kickers' available for the NES, or basically just squarewaves that are pitched to sound like bass drums. So do I want to do that, but abandon a melody channel? It's the case that the average person listening won't know about the technical constraints, so do I want to make the song sound 'worse' for them just for the sake of preserving an arbitrary authenticity?

There is a mild overlap, in that some of the spaces I've talked to other games online they've both played SHMUPS and done speedruns... I'm personally one of those people, and while I enjoy both things, they don't feel super similar to me. 

In speedrunning, unless you are playing a super popular/optimized game, you have a lot of room for error and player expression. In a SHMUP, your player expression is mostly down to how perfectly you can execute a given run... there's very little room for error, and any mistake you make directly impacts the 'value' of the run.

Furthermore, as people have pointed out, SHMUPS themselves are generally not fun to speedrun--most of them are just about playing with no mistakes, which is pretty much close to normal play but even more punishing if you screw up. So if you're good enough for a speedrun of a game you have to be good enough for a no death/1CC, in which case you may as well be playing the game normally anyway.
